Q1.text: A serious problem has come up in your family or among people close to you. What do you do first?

opts.t: I try to understand exactly how this situation arose and what factors led to it
I think about what can be done right now to move forward
I say out loud what everyone is silent about — without that the conversation won't move
I want to understand what this situation means for each of the people close to me

Q1.text: You're offered something completely new to you. Your first reaction:

opts.t: I see several possibilities — and I want to get started
I immediately see where the promise and the reality diverge — and I want to clear that up
I want to understand why this matters and what it will change for people
I want to figure out how it works — its logic and structure

Q1.text: A friend tells you about a difficult situation in their life. You:

opts.t: I notice they are steering around the main thing — and I name it gently
First, I want to understand what they're feeling and what this situation means to them
I try to understand the structure of the problem — what led to it and how it works
I think about what specifically can be done to change the situation

Q1.text: A meeting didn't go the way you planned. What do you think about afterward?

opts.t: I think about what was left unsaid and what this meeting meant for the people involved
I want to understand why it turned out that way — the logic behind what happened
I think about what needs to change next time to get a different result
I see specific mistakes that could have been avoided — and that will likely happen again

Q1.text: You read about a difficult situation that happened to people you don't know. What interests you most?

opts.t: Exactly how it all worked, and why the situation unfolded the way it did
What they could have done differently, and what applies to my own life
What was obvious in this situation but that everyone preferred not to notice
What it meant for the people involved — how they experienced it

Q1.text: You need to make an important decision under uncertainty. You:

opts.t: Choose the most promising option and start moving — you'll figure it out along the way
Check which assumptions behind the options are left unnamed — those are usually what fail
Think about which decision will be aligned with your values
Gather more information to better understand the situation

Q1.text: A conflict has come up among friends or in your family. Your role in it:

opts.t: I name what others avoid saying out loud — even if it's uncomfortable
I try to understand what's behind each person's position and create space for dialogue
I try to work out the causes and understand how this conflict came about
I want to find a solution quickly and move on

Q1.text: You learn about a new idea or concept. What happens next?

opts.t: I think about what meaning it carries and how it changes my understanding of the world
I want to understand its logic and structure — how it works on the inside
I immediately think about where and how it could be applied
I notice where there are contradictions or weak points in it

Q1.text: You're finishing a major undertaking you put a lot of effort into. What do you feel first?

opts.t: I want to understand what went well in this, what didn't, and why
I'm already thinking about the next step — what can be done next
I see what could have been done better — and what got in the way of that
I think about what this meant for me and for the people I did it with

Q1.text: Someone tells you about a person you don't know. What interests you most?

opts.t: What they do and what they've achieved
How well their words match their actions
What matters to them and what drives them
How they think and the logic behind their actions

Q1.text: You're preparing for an important conversation. You spend most of your time on:

opts.t: Preparing arguments about what's going wrong and why it matters to change it
Understanding what matters to the other person and what this conversation means for both of you
Understanding the context and logic of the situation — what led to it
Thinking through exactly what you want to propose or change

Q1.text: You've received unexpected feedback about yourself. Your first reaction:

opts.t: I think about what this feedback means for my understanding of myself
I want to understand what this assessment is based on and how objective it is
I think about what specifically I can change in my behavior
I check how honest this feedback is and whether it contradicts other facts

Q1.text: You see that a plan isn't working. What do you do?

opts.t: I analyze exactly where it broke down and why
I quickly adapt the plan and keep moving
I say plainly where the plan didn't add up from the start — so the next one doesn't repeat it
I think about what this situation teaches us and what's important to hold on to

Q1.text: You're studying a new field. How do you go about it?

opts.t: I try applying it right away — I learn by doing, filling in the gaps as I go
I go where the experts disagree — that's where you see what is actually still unsettled
I look for meaning and a connection to what already matters to me
Systematically — I build understanding from fundamentals to details

Q1.text: In a conversation, you notice the other person is saying one thing but means another. You:

opts.t: I name the contradiction directly — it matters for an honest conversation
I try to understand what they're actually feeling and what they don't dare say
I try to understand what's behind their words — the logic of their position
I focus on what can be done about what they actually want

Q1.text: You need to explain a complex idea to someone else. You:

opts.t: I look for an image or story that will resonate and bring the idea to life
I build the explanation from logic to detail — structure first, then the parts
I show, with an example, how it works in practice
I first separate what is easy to confuse — otherwise the idea lands on the wrong footing

Q1.text: You watch a group of people making a decision. What do you notice first?

opts.t: The logic of the process — how the discussion is structured and what the arguments are based on
Whether the group has a sense of the next step and is moving toward a result
The gap between what is agreed out loud and what actually decides the outcome
How the people feel during this process

Q1.text: You're going through a difficult period in your life. What helps you move forward?

opts.t: Focusing on concrete steps — what I can do right now
Clarity about exactly what went wrong and what needs to change
Understanding the meaning of what's happening — why it's happening and what it teaches
Understanding how this situation is put together and what its causes are

Q1.text: You're taking part in a discussion of a shared plan. Your main contribution:

opts.t: I point out weak spots and assumptions that could turn into problems
I raise the question of what this plan is for — why we're doing this
I ask questions about how everything connects — I look for the logic
I suggest concrete steps and entry points — where we could start right now

Q1.text: You hear a story about someone's success. What interests you most?

opts.t: What this experience meant for the person — how it changed them
Exactly how it was achieved — the logic of the path they took
What from this can be applied to my own situation
What's actually behind this success

Q1.text: You need to write an important letter. Where do you start?

opts.t: With logic — I build the structure of the arguments first
With the main conclusion — what I want the person to do after reading it
With whatever could be read two ways — I remove the places where the meaning can be swapped
With what the reader will feel — what tone will create the right connection

Q1.text: A project you're involved in is moving in the wrong direction. You:

opts.t: I propose a concrete change of course and am willing to take responsibility for it
I say plainly that the direction is wrong — and explain why
I raise the question of what we're doing all this for
I first want to understand at what point and why the shift happened

Q1.text: You find out that someone you trusted acted dishonestly. Your first reaction:

opts.t: This confirms what I'd noticed — and what should have been named sooner
I feel the break in trust — I think about what this means for our relationship
I want to understand how this became possible — what I missed
I think about what needs to change in the situation to move forward

Q1.text: At the end of the day, you think about what happened. What occupies your thoughts?

opts.t: I think about what was real in this day — what actually mattered
I try to connect the events of the day into a single picture — what led to what
I think about what moved forward and what needs to happen tomorrow
I notice where words and deeds parted ways today — mine and other people's

Q2.text: Past failures continue to affect how I make decisions today.
When something goes wrong, I tend to think that's just how it always goes for me.
Painful past experiences often get in the way of me acting confidently in the present.
Memories of good times give me support when things are difficult now.
Past experience is my main resource — that's where I find what works.
I like revisiting stories from my life — they help me understand who I am.
I rarely believe I can significantly change what happens in my life.
What happens to me often feels like the result of circumstances rather than my own decisions.
There's no point planning for the future — things never turn out the way they're planned anyway.
I live in the present moment — and I find it hard to think about the consequences of the distant future.
Spontaneous decisions often turn out to be the best ones — it's better to act than to plan.
It matters to me to enjoy what's happening right now.
I often think about what I want to achieve — and I build concrete plans for it.
My decisions today are shaped by where I want to be in the future.
I'm willing to give up immediate pleasure for a long-term result.

Q3.text: When I tell someone what happened, it feels like I'm just stating the facts — not my own version of events.
When something keeps repeating in my life, it feels more like a feature of the world or other people than my own habitual reactions.
When someone sees the same situation completely differently than I do, I find it hard to understand how that's possible.
I notice that I react in roughly the same way in similar situations — and I can name it.
I can see the difference between what happened and what I think about it.
Sometimes I catch myself reacting out of habit — even though the situation might call for a different approach.
When I deliberately look at a situation from a different angle, my reaction actually changes.
Once I understand which habitual script is kicking in, I can choose to act differently.
I regularly track my habitual ways of explaining what happens — and change them when they're not helping me.
I can see how my personal beliefs are connected to the beliefs of the group or culture I grew up in.
I know how to work with other people's habitual reactions and beliefs — not just my own.
I can calmly hold the tension between different points of view without rushing to resolve it immediately.
